items.a03-h: Eli Raz, Man of the Desert and the Dead Sea
items.a03-p002: I came to know Eli sometime in the late seventies, when I was appointed director of the Sde Boker Field School and Eli was nearing the end of his work at the Ein Gedi Field School. Until then he had taught the geology unit of the guide-training courses of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, and I stepped into his shoes.
items.a03-p003: In his research for his master's thesis, Eli unravelled one of the secrets (raz) of the geology of the Judaean Desert, a riddle that until then had remained unexplained: he put forward a model for the development of the dolomite plates of the Judaean Desert, and we used this model in our guiding in the area.
items.a03-p004: In 1989 Eli asked me to join his team in a cross-Negev motor navigation contest, "Rally – To the Negev". I may admit that I was greatly flattered by the offer. For two or three days we ploughed the dust roads of the Negev, and each of us displayed his deep familiarity with the secrets (raz) of the desert.
items.a03-p005: In the early 2000s the government charged the Ministry of Environmental Protection with preparing a policy document on the future of the Dead Sea, centred on an analysis of how the drop in the level of the sea affects its surroundings. The document drew up a series of recommendations to the government on how to act in the region, in the near and in the distant future.
items.a03-p006: I headed the team together with a few colleagues. At the start of the work we recruited experts from various fields of knowledge to the team. Eli, who knows the Dead Sea and its shores like the back of his hand, was among the first we recruited. In the course of the work discussions were held, the members of the <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-14" title="10"/>team learned from one another, and we drew up recommendations to the government. Some of the recommendations contradicted (to put it mildly) the development policy prepared by those at the helm of the Tamar Regional Council. Eli found himself in an awkward position with neighbours and close friends, when he had to confront their view of the world. But he held to his professional positions and stood his ground. At one of the meetings before the position paper was signed, the head of the regional council at the time, Dov Litvinoff, said a sentence that changed how the council saw the paper: from a hostile document to one whose conclusions should be adopted for the sake of a sensible development of the region. This is what he said: "Like a mirror set up before us, it is hard for us to accept the reality reflected before our eyes. A reality we did not know, and one that must be built into the planning of the region's future."
items.a03-p007: Geologists characterise a rock by the mix of minerals that make it up. In my eyes, Eli is a mix of a triad of components: the Dead Sea man, the geologist of the dolomite plates, and the exacting guide and educator who heeds the saying "Practise what you preach!" He sees broad horizons with soaring vision, but is exacting in the details.
